The real issue isn’t the bill’s intent—it’s the systemic rot in healthcare spending. New York’s Medicaid program hemorrhages billions through pharma overpayments, bloated admin costs, and consultant kickbacks. The Essential Plan? A Band-Aid on a bullet wound.

Premium spikes happen when D.C. prioritizes insurance middlemen over patients. True reform means slashing Big Pharma’s taxpayer-funded handouts, ending $200B in Medicare fraud, and forcing hospitals to compete on price.

Until then, every “cut” just shifts costs from bureaucrats to families. Fix the disease, not the symptoms.

The Medicare Home Health Accessibility Act (H.R. 2013) exemplifies misplaced priorities disguised as reform. While occupational therapy has value, expanding Medicare coverage for behavioral health through bureaucratic mechanisms ignores systemic failures. The bill amends Social Security Act sections to broaden eligibility but does nothing to address Medicaid’s $98B annual fraud problem or hospital price-gouging that drives up costs.

Real solutions require dismantling bloated administrative structures and redirecting funds to patient-centered care—not layering more complexity onto a broken system.

Washington keeps throwing cash at symptoms while ignoring the disease: a healthcare-industrial complex that profits from inefficiency.
